correctness.rationale: The surviving Fourier Vandermonde is square and nonsingular by root count. An n-point DFT leaves only the two complementary frequencies, so the two zeros determine a unique shifted cosine. Elementary sign comparison gives precisely delta-1 negative weights; finite cosine sums give sharp negative mass; Fourier orthogonality gives exact squared norm. A cosecant-squared identity and uniform pair counting give the stated random-erasure expectation. A continuous-mapping argument and explicit inversion give the heavy-tail law. Finite cross-checks test 14,235 cases and 98 averages, not the infinite statement.

value.rationale: The near-Nyquist erasure problem is a natural exact quadrature robustness question: only two lost sites cause an explicitly quantified probability of sign failure, arbitrarily large worst-case sample-noise amplification, and a nonvanishing expected noise variance as the grid grows. These exact structural obstructions matter for sensor-dropout quadrature and distinguish exact integration from noise robustness.
